title: Light, Lenses and Signals
bigQuestion: How do people use waves to see what is too small, too far or too dark for the eye, and to send a picture around the world in a second?

story.title: Four New Stars Beside Jupiter
story.kicker: One cold January night in 1610, a tube with two pieces of glass changed what the sky was allowed to be.
paragraphs: On the evening of January 7, 1610, Galileo Galilei climbed to a window in Padua, Italy, and pointed a homemade tube at Jupiter. The tube was a spyglass. Word had come from the Netherlands a year earlier that a lens maker had put two glass lenses in a tube and made distant church towers leap closer. Galileo ground his own lenses, improved the design, and built one that made things look about 20 times larger.

Jupiter itself was a small bright disc. But beside it, in a neat line, sat three tiny points of light that no chart showed. Galileo assumed they were faint background stars. The next night he looked again, and the three points had moved. Stars do not do that. On later nights a fourth appeared, and the four little lights shifted from side to side of Jupiter, sometimes vanishing behind it, always staying near.

By the middle of January he was sure. These were not stars. They were moons circling Jupiter, the way our moon circles Earth. That mattered enormously. Many scholars still taught that everything in the heavens circled Earth. Here were four objects plainly circling something else. Galileo rushed a small book into print that March, and readers across Europe lined up to buy spyglasses of their own.

The instrument that made this possible was nothing but refraction. One lens gathered far more light than a human pupil could and bent it to a focus. A second lens spread that focused light so the eye could inspect it. Two curved pieces of glass, and a whole planet's family came into view. This chapter is about what people have built since: microscopes, telescopes, cameras, fiber cables and radar, all ways of using waves to carry information the unaided senses could never catch.
story.think: Galileo trusted a brand-new instrument over centuries of teaching. What made his observation convincing enough to change minds, and what could a critic have said back?

lessons.title: What a Lens Does
lessons.mainIdea: A convex lens refracts parallel light rays to a focal point, and objects placed near it appear magnified.
reading: Hold a magnifying glass over a sidewalk on a sunny day and slide it up and down. At one height the sunlight collapses into a tiny, painfully bright spot. That spot is the *focal point*, and its distance from the lens is the *focal length*. The lens is convex, thicker in the middle, so every part of it bends the incoming light toward the center. Parallel rays from the sun meet at one place.

Now hold the same lens over a printed page, closer than its focal length. The letters swell. You are looking at a *magnified* image, larger than the object. The rays leaving each letter are bent by the lens so that, when they reach your eye, they seem to come from a much bigger letter farther away. The eye and brain cannot tell the difference between real rays and bent ones, so you see a giant letter.

A fatter lens, with more curve, has a shorter focal length and magnifies more. But it also blurs and colors the edges of the image. Early lens makers fought these flaws for centuries. Wider lenses gather more light. That is why a telescope lens is much bigger than a magnifying glass. The point is not just to enlarge. It is to collect enough dim light from a distant object to see it at all.

words.d: the spot where a lens brings parallel light rays together
the distance from a lens to its focal point
made to look larger than the real object

look.title: The Water Drop Lens
look.text: A student places a single drop of water on a clear plastic sheet and lays it over a page of newsprint. Through the drop, the letters underneath look noticeably bigger. When she flattens the drop by pressing it, the letters shrink back toward normal size.
look.prompt: Why does a round drop of water work as a lens? What about pressing it flat changed the magnification?

check.q: What is the focal point of a convex lens?
choices: The place where parallel rays are brought together
The center of the lens
The point where light is absorbed
The edge where light bends most
check.why: A convex lens bends parallel rays inward so they meet at one spot, the focal point.

check.q: Why does a magnifying glass make letters look bigger?
choices: It makes the letters physically larger
It bends the rays so they seem to come from a larger, farther object
It adds light to the page
It reflects the letters back at your eye
check.why: The lens refracts the rays leaving each letter. To the eye, the bent rays appear to come from a bigger letter.

check.q: Why are telescope lenses made much wider than a magnifying glass?
choices: Wider glass is cheaper
Wide lenses bend light less
A wider lens gathers more of the faint light from distant objects
Wide lenses do not need to be curved
check.why: Distant objects send very little light. A large lens collects more of it, making faint things bright enough to see.

lessons.title: Inside a Microscope
lessons.mainIdea: A compound microscope uses two lenses in a row, so the magnification of one is multiplied by the magnification of the other.
reading: The site's microscope has two sets of lenses. Nearest the specimen is the *objective* lens, a small, strongly curved lens that sits a few millimeters above the glass slide. It forms a magnified image of the specimen inside the tube. At the top is the *eyepiece*, which you look through. It acts like a magnifying glass on the image the objective already made. Two enlargements in a row multiply: a 10x objective and a 10x eyepiece give 100x.

Light matters as much as glass. A mirror or lamp under the stage sends light up through the thin specimen. What you see is light transmitted through the sample, with dark parts where cells absorb it. That is why a slice must be very thin. It is also why stains are used. A dye that a cell nucleus absorbs turns the nucleus dark and visible.

In 1665 Robert Hooke published a book of drawings made with a two-lens microscope, including a thin slice of cork that looked like rows of tiny boxes. He called them cells. The name stuck to the units of every living thing. A few years later, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek in the Netherlands used single, tiny, very powerful lenses to see living things in pond water that nobody had known were there.

Light microscopes have a hard limit. Visible light has a wavelength of around 500 nanometers, and anything much smaller than that wavelength simply cannot be resolved by light, no matter how good the glass. Seeing viruses or atoms took a different kind of wave, and electron microscopes in the twentieth century supplied it.

words.d: the lens of a microscope or telescope nearest the object, which forms the first image
the lens you look through, which magnifies the image made by the objective
the sample being examined

look.title: Hooke Looks at Cork
look.text: Hooke wrote that when he cut a thin slice of cork with a sharp penknife and placed it under his microscope, he could see that it was full of tiny pores or boxes, which he compared to a honeycomb. He counted them and estimated that more than a thousand million could fit in a cubic inch. He called these little spaces cells.
look.prompt: Hooke was looking at dead cork, not living cells. Why do you think he chose the word cell, and what did he get right and wrong?

check.q: A microscope has a 40x objective and a 10x eyepiece. Its total magnification is:
choices: 4x
check.why: The eyepiece magnifies the image the objective already made, so the two numbers multiply: 40 times 10 is 400.

check.q: Why must a specimen for a light microscope be cut very thin?
choices: So light can pass through it to the lens
So it fits under the eyepiece
So the stain dries faster
So the objective does not magnify it too much
check.why: The image is made from light transmitted through the sample. A thick slice blocks the light and shows only a dark blob.

check.q: Why can a light microscope not show an individual virus clearly?
choices: Viruses are transparent
Viruses are smaller than the wavelength of visible light
The eyepiece is too weak
Viruses move too fast
check.why: Light cannot resolve details much smaller than its own wavelength, about 500 nanometers. Most viruses are far smaller than that.

lessons.title: Telescopes: Lenses vs Mirrors
lessons.mainIdea: Early telescopes used lenses; large modern telescopes use curved mirrors, which can be built far bigger and gather far more light.
reading: Galileo's telescope was a *refractor*: a large lens at the front gathered light and a small lens at the back magnified it. Refractors improved for nearly three centuries. The largest ever put into regular use is at Yerkes Observatory in Williams Bay, Wisconsin, a two-hour drive from Chicago. Its lens, finished in 1897, is 40 inches, about 1 meter, across. Nobody built a bigger one, because a glass lens that large sags under its own weight and blurs.

The answer was a mirror. In 1668 Isaac Newton built a small telescope that used a curved mirror instead of a front lens. A mirror can be supported from behind, so it can be made huge, and it reflects every color to the same focus, avoiding the color fringes that lenses add. Nearly every large telescope since has been a *reflector*. The Hale telescope on Palomar Mountain, California, finished in 1948, has a mirror about 5 meters across.

Two more problems remained: air and daylight. Earth's atmosphere wobbles, making stars twinkle and images shimmer. The Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990 with a 2.4-meter mirror, solved both by orbiting above the air. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched on December 25, 2021, carries a 6.5-meter mirror built from 18 gold-coated hexagons that unfolded in space. It sees in infrared, a kind of light explained in the next section.

Chicago has its own place in this story. The Adler Planetarium on the lakefront, opened in 1930, was the first planetarium in the Western Hemisphere. And every telescope, from Galileo's tube to Webb, works on the same two ideas from the last chapter: gather as much light as possible, and bend it to a focus.

words.d: a telescope that gathers light with a large lens
a telescope that gathers light with a curved mirror
the layer of air around Earth, which blurs and dims starlight

look.title: How Wide Is the Light Collector?
look.cite: observatory and NASA published values, rounded
look.prompt: Hubble's mirror is smaller than Hale's, yet Hubble produced sharper pictures. What did Hubble have that Hale did not?

check.q: Why did astronomers stop building larger refracting telescopes after about 1 meter?
choices: Lenses became too expensive to ship
Larger lenses were not allowed by law
A huge glass lens sags under its own weight and blurs the image
Larger lenses gather too much light
check.why: A lens can only be held at its edge. Past about a meter, its own weight bends it out of shape.

check.q: What is the main advantage of a mirror over a lens for a big telescope?
choices: Mirrors are always lighter than air
Mirrors magnify more
Mirrors do not need to be curved
A mirror can be supported from behind, so it can be made very large
check.why: Support from behind lets a mirror be huge without sagging, and mirrors also avoid color fringes.

check.q: Why does placing a telescope in orbit improve its images?
choices: It is above the atmosphere, which blurs and dims starlight
It is closer to the stars
Space is warmer than a mountaintop
Gravity is stronger in orbit
check.why: Earth's moving air makes images shimmer. Above it, a telescope sees steady, unblurred light.

lessons.title: Light Beyond the Rainbow
lessons.mainIdea: Visible light is only a small slice of a much wider family of electromagnetic waves, discovered one piece at a time.
reading: In 1800 the astronomer William Herschel spread sunlight into a rainbow with a prism and set a thermometer in each color. Red warmed the thermometer more than violet. Then he tried something odd: he moved the thermometer past the red end, into what looked like empty shadow. It got warmer still. Something invisible was arriving there, carrying energy. He had found *infrared* light, light with a wavelength too long for the eye.

A year later Johann Ritter tried the other end. Paper soaked in silver chloride darkens in light. Ritter found it darkened fastest just beyond the violet, where nothing could be seen. That was *ultraviolet*. Over the next century the family kept growing. In 1887 Heinrich Hertz made and detected radio waves in his lab. In 1895 Wilhelm Röntgen found X-rays, which passed through flesh and cast shadows of bone.

All of these are the same kind of wave as visible light. They are electromagnetic waves traveling at the same speed, differing only in wavelength and frequency. Lined up from longest wavelength to shortest, they make the *electromagnetic spectrum*: radio, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays. Visible light, from about 700 down to 400 nanometers, is a thin sliver near the middle. Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and more energy per wave. That is why ultraviolet burns skin and radio waves do not.

words.d: electromagnetic waves with wavelengths a little longer than red light; felt as heat
electromagnetic waves with wavelengths a little shorter than violet light; can burn skin
the whole range of electromagnetic waves, from radio to gamma rays, ordered by wavelength

look.title: Herschel's Thermometer in the Dark
look.text: Herschel described placing thermometers in the different colors of a spectrum cast by a prism and found that the heating increased from violet toward red. Moving a thermometer beyond the red, where no light was visible, he found the temperature rose even more, and he concluded that the sun sends out invisible rays that carry heat.
look.cite: William Herschel, paper read to the Royal Society, 1800
look.prompt: Herschel used a thermometer instead of his eyes as the detector. Why was that choice the key to the discovery?

check.q: How did Herschel find infrared light?
choices: He saw a dark red glow beyond the rainbow
A thermometer placed beyond the red end of a spectrum warmed up
He photographed it
He heard it on a radio
check.why: Infrared is invisible, but it carries energy. The thermometer detected the energy where his eyes saw nothing.

check.q: Which of these has the shortest wavelength?
choices: Radio waves
Infrared
X-rays
Visible light
check.why: The spectrum runs from long radio waves through visible light to short X-rays and gamma rays.

check.q: Why can ultraviolet light burn skin while radio waves cannot?
choices: Ultraviolet travels faster
Ultraviolet is louder
Radio waves are absorbed by clouds
Ultraviolet has a higher frequency and more energy per wave
check.why: All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed. Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and more energy.

lessons.title: Waves We Use Every Day
lessons.mainIdea: Different parts of the spectrum do different jobs, from radio for broadcasting to X-rays for seeing bones, based on what each wavelength passes through or is absorbed by.
reading: Look around a kitchen and count the spectrum. The radio on the counter picks up FM signals near 100 megahertz, waves about 3 meters long that bend around buildings. The microwave oven fills its box with waves about 12 centimeters long that water absorbs strongly, so the food heats from the water inside it while the dry plate stays cool. The toaster glows with infrared. The overhead lamp gives visible light. Each job uses the wavelength that behaves the right way.

*Radio waves*, the longest, pass through walls and travel far. That makes them ideal for broadcasting and for cell phones, whose signals sit between a few hundred megahertz and a few gigahertz. *Microwaves* are shorter and can be aimed in tight beams, useful for radar and for Wi-Fi. Infrared cameras see warm bodies in the dark, because everything warm gives off infrared. Ultraviolet from the sun tans and burns. Sunscreen absorbs it before the skin does.

*X-rays* pass easily through soft tissue but are absorbed by bone. So a bone casts a shadow on the film or sensor. Gamma rays, the most energetic, come from radioactive atoms and are used in some cancer treatments. Higher-frequency waves carry more energy, so X-rays and gamma rays can damage cells. That is why a dentist steps out of the room and a lead apron covers your chest.

words.d: the longest electromagnetic waves, used for broadcasting and phone signals
electromagnetic waves shorter than radio waves, used for cooking, radar and Wi-Fi
high-energy electromagnetic waves that pass through soft tissue but not bone

look.title: Frequencies of Some Everyday Radio Signals
look.prompt: Which of these signals has the longest wavelength? Why would a long wavelength help a signal reach a radio in a basement?

check.q: Why does a microwave oven heat the food but leave a dry plate cool?
choices: Microwaves are absorbed by water in the food, not by the dry plate
The plate reflects heat back into the food
The food is closer to the light bulb
Plates are made of metal
check.why: The oven's wavelength is chosen because water absorbs it strongly. The plate has no water, so it stays cool.

check.q: Why do bones show up on an X-ray image?
choices: Bones glow when hit by X-rays
Bones absorb X-rays while soft tissue lets them pass
Bones reflect X-rays back to the camera
Bones are colder than muscle
check.why: X-rays pass through soft tissue but are stopped by dense bone, so bone casts a shadow on the detector.

check.q: Which part of the spectrum lets an infrared camera see a person in complete darkness?
choices: Reflected moonlight
Radio waves from the person's phone
Infrared given off by the warm body
Ultraviolet from the skin
check.why: Anything warm emits infrared. The camera detects that emitted radiation, with no visible light needed.

lessons.title: Seeing in Other Light
lessons.mainIdea: Telescopes that detect infrared, radio or X-rays reveal objects and events that visible light cannot show.
reading: The universe does not shine only in colors we can see. Clouds of dust that block visible light are nearly transparent to infrared. So an infrared telescope can look straight through them at the stars forming inside. The James Webb Space Telescope was built for exactly this. Its mirror is coated in a thin layer of gold, because gold reflects infrared very well. The whole telescope hides behind a sunshield the size of a tennis court, so its own warmth does not blind it.

There is a second reason Webb sees in infrared. The universe is expanding. Light from the most distant galaxies has been stretched during its long trip, shifting visible light into the infrared. Catching that stretched light lets Webb see galaxies as they were more than 13 billion years ago, when the universe was young. A telescope is a kind of time machine. The farther away it looks, the further back in time it sees.

Radio telescopes, huge dish antennas, map cold hydrogen gas and the leftover glow of the early universe. X-ray telescopes in orbit catch the light from gas heated to millions of degrees near black holes. Each window in the spectrum shows a different universe. Astronomers combine them into one picture. A doctor does the same with an X-ray, an ultrasound and a photograph of one patient.

words.d: a set of thin layers that block the sun's heat and light from a space telescope
an enormous group of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity

look.title: NASA on Why Webb Sees Infrared
look.text: NASA explains that Webb observes in infrared for two main reasons. Light from the earliest galaxies has been stretched by the expansion of the universe into infrared wavelengths, so only an infrared telescope can catch it. And infrared passes through the clouds of dust where stars and planets form, letting the telescope see inside regions that hide from visible-light telescopes.
look.cite: NASA, James Webb Space Telescope science overview
look.prompt: Why does Webb need to stay very cold, and how does the sunshield help with that?

check.q: Why is Webb's mirror coated with gold?
choices: Gold is the strongest metal
Gold is heavier and steadier
Gold absorbs infrared
Gold reflects infrared light very well
check.why: Webb collects infrared. Gold is an excellent infrared reflector, so the coating sends that light to the detectors.

check.q: Why can an infrared telescope see stars forming inside a dust cloud?
choices: Infrared passes through dust that blocks visible light
Infrared is brighter than visible light
Dust clouds glow in visible light
Infrared travels faster through dust
check.why: Dust grains scatter visible light strongly but let longer infrared waves pass, so the stars inside show through.

check.q: Why is looking at a very distant galaxy also looking into the past?
choices: Distant galaxies move backward in time
Its light took billions of years to arrive, so we see it as it was when the light left
Telescopes slow down light
Galaxies stop changing after they form
check.why: Light travels at a fixed speed. Light from a galaxy 13 billion light-years away left it 13 billion years ago.

lessons.title: Analog and Digital
lessons.mainIdea: An analog signal copies a wave's shape directly, while a digital signal turns it into numbers, which resist noise and copy perfectly.
reading: The groove on a vinyl record is an *analog* signal. Its wiggle is a direct copy of the sound wave's shape: twice as loud, twice as wide. That is simple and elegant, but it has a weakness. Every scratch, every speck of dust, every bit of wear adds its own wiggle, and the player cannot tell the added wiggle from the music. Copy an analog tape to another tape and the hiss of the first copy is copied too, plus new hiss. After a few generations the music is buried.

A *digital* signal takes a different route. Thousands of times a second, it measures the wave's height and writes the measurement down as a number. Each number is stored as a string of *bits*, ones and zeros. A CD samples the wave 44,100 times each second. Instead of a shape, the recording is a long list of numbers.

Numbers can be protected in a way shapes cannot. A one is sent as a high voltage or a bright flash, a zero as a low voltage or darkness. Noise may nudge a high signal a little lower or a low signal a little higher, but as long as the receiver can still tell high from low, it reads the bit correctly and the noise vanishes. Extra check bits let the receiver notice and fix bits that did get flipped. A digital file copied a million times is still exactly the same file.

This is why phone calls, streaming music, photographs and this web page are all digital. The trade-off is that a digital recording only keeps what it measured. Sample too rarely or store too few bits per sample and the sound gets coarse. Engineers choose sample rates high enough that the ear cannot tell the difference.

words.d: a signal that copies the shape of the original wave directly
a signal made of numbers, stored as ones and zeros
a single one or zero, the smallest piece of digital information
unwanted random changes added to a signal

look.title: Passing a Message Down a Line
look.text: Two classes play a game. In the first, a student draws a curvy line on paper and each person in a row copies the drawing by hand and passes their copy on. In the second, a student writes the numbers 3, 7, 2, 9 and each person copies the numbers. After twenty copies, the drawings barely resemble the original, but the numbers are still 3, 7, 2, 9.
look.prompt: Which class was passing an analog signal and which a digital one? Why did the numbers survive when the drawing did not?

check.q: What is the main weakness of an analog signal?
choices: It cannot record music
It uses too many numbers
Noise gets added and cannot be separated from the signal
It travels more slowly than a digital one
check.why: An analog signal is a shape. Any scratch or hiss changes the shape, and the player cannot tell which wiggle was the original.

check.q: Why can a digital signal ignore small amounts of noise?
choices: Digital signals are louder
Digital signals carry no energy
Noise cannot touch a digital wire
The receiver only has to tell a high from a low, and small nudges do not change that
check.why: Each bit is either high or low. As long as noise does not push one across to the other, the bit reads correctly and the noise is discarded.

check.q: What is a bit?
choices: A single one or zero
One second of sound
One wiggle in a record groove
A small scratch on a disc
check.why: A bit is the smallest unit of digital information: one binary digit, either 1 or 0.

lessons.title: How a Phone Sends a Picture
lessons.mainIdea: A phone turns a picture into millions of numbers, sends them as bits over radio waves and cables, and the receiving phone rebuilds the image from the numbers.
reading: You take a photo of the Bean in Millennium Park and tap send. Inside the camera, a grid of millions of tiny light sensors, one per *pixel*, has measured how much red, green and blue light landed on it. Each color is stored as a number from 0 to 255, so each pixel is three numbers, and each number is 8 bits. A 12-million-pixel picture is nearly 300 million bits before anything else happens.

That is too much to send quickly, so the phone *compresses* the image. It looks for patches where neighboring pixels are nearly the same color, such as the sky, and stores a short description instead of every value. A typical photo shrinks to a few million bits with almost no visible loss. The file is then chopped into packets, each labeled with where it belongs.

The phone's antenna sends the packets as radio waves to a cell tower that may be a kilometer away. The wave is switched on and off, or shifted slightly, to mean one or zero. From the tower the bits usually travel by glass fiber, as pulses of light. They pass through switching centers, possibly across an ocean, to the tower nearest your friend. Her phone receives the radio packets and checks each one for errors. It asks again for any that were damaged, then rebuilds the numbers.

Finally her screen does the reverse of your camera: at each pixel it lights three tiny red, green and blue elements to the strength the numbers say. The whole trip takes about a second, and nothing physical made the journey. Only a pattern did, exactly as with the ripple on the pond in the last chapter.

words.d: one tiny square of a digital image, stored as numbers for red, green and blue
to shrink a file by storing repeated or predictable parts more briefly
a small labeled chunk of a digital message sent separately and reassembled

look.title: The Photo That Arrived Blocky
look.text: A student sends a photo of a sunset over Lake Michigan while riding a train through a tunnel. The picture arrives, but the sky looks like large flat squares instead of a smooth gradient, and a friend asks why it looks so much worse than the original.
look.prompt: The phone chose a stronger compression because the connection was weak. Using what you know about pixels and compression, explain why the sky turned into squares.

check.q: In a digital photo, what is stored for each pixel?
choices: The name of the color
Numbers for how much red, green and blue light was measured
A tiny copy of the whole image
A sound wave
check.why: Each pixel's color is recorded as three numbers, typically 0 to 255 each, for red, green and blue.

check.q: Why does a phone compress a photo before sending it?
choices: To make the colors brighter
To add error-checking bits
To shrink the number of bits so it sends faster
To turn it from digital into analog
check.why: A raw image is hundreds of millions of bits. Compression stores repeated areas briefly, cutting the size many times over.

check.q: Which two carriers usually take the bits between your phone and a distant friend's phone?
choices: Sound waves and water pipes
Copper wire the whole way
Infrared and ultraviolet beams
Radio waves to the tower, then light pulses in glass fiber
check.why: Phones talk to towers by radio. Between towers and across long distances, the bits ride as light in fiber-optic cables.

lessons.title: Light in a Glass Thread
lessons.mainIdea: Optical fiber traps light inside a hair-thin strand of glass by total internal reflection and carries digital signals across oceans.
reading: Aim a flashlight up from under water at a shallow angle and the light does not leave the pool. It bounces off the surface as if the surface were a mirror. This is *total internal reflection*. Light moving from a slower material such as water or glass toward a faster one such as air is bent away from the surface, and past a certain angle it cannot escape at all. It reflects back in, losing almost nothing.

An *optical fiber* uses this trick on purpose. It is a strand of extremely pure glass thinner than a human hair. It is wrapped in a second glass layer that light travels through faster. Light pulses entering one end glance off the boundary again and again, tens of thousands of times per kilometer. They stay trapped in the core until they come out the far end. A laser flashes on for a one and off for a zero, billions of times each second.

Fiber beats copper wire in every way that matters for signals. The glass is so pure that a pulse can travel 100 kilometers before it needs a boost. A window pane that pure would let you see clearly through a stack a kilometer thick. Light pulses do not interfere with each other the way electric currents in nearby wires do. One fiber can carry many colors at once, each color a separate stream of bits. Undersea fiber cables now carry nearly all international internet traffic. The first was laid across the Atlantic in 1988.

The idea reaches back to 1880. That year Alexander Graham Bell sent a voice a few hundred meters on a beam of sunlight, with a device he called the photophone. Clouds blocked it, so it was never practical. Glass gave the light a protected road. In 1966 the engineer Charles Kao showed that glass pure enough could make that road span the world.

words.d: when light inside a slower material hits the boundary at a shallow angle and reflects completely instead of escaping
a hair-thin strand of very pure glass that carries light signals by trapping them inside
a device that produces a narrow, single-color beam of light

look.title: Bell Hears Sunlight Speak
look.text: In a letter written in 1880, Bell told his father that he had managed to make a beam of sunlight carry his voice. He wrote with excitement that he had heard speech produced by sunlight and had heard a sunbeam laugh, cough and sing, and he thought this photophone might be his greatest invention.
look.cite: Alexander Graham Bell, letter to his father, 1880
look.prompt: Bell's photophone worked but was never widely used. What problem did optical fiber solve that Bell could not?

check.q: What keeps light trapped inside an optical fiber?
choices: Total internal reflection at the boundary of the glass core
A metal coating that absorbs stray light
Mirrors placed every meter
The light is too slow to escape
check.why: Light hits the boundary between core and outer layer at a shallow angle and reflects fully back inside, over and over.

check.q: How is a one or a zero sent down a fiber?
choices: As a high or low sound
As a flash of light on or off
As a red or blue color
As a thick or thin strand
check.why: A laser turns on for a one and off for a zero, billions of times per second, and the pulses travel through the glass.

check.q: Why can one fiber carry many separate streams of bits at the same time?
choices: The fiber is very wide
The bits travel at different speeds
Different colors of light travel in the same fiber without mixing
Each stream uses a different tower
check.why: Different wavelengths of light do not interfere with one another, so each color can carry its own signal through the same strand.

lessons.title: Sonar and the Bat
lessons.mainIdea: Sonar and echolocation send out sound and time the echo, using the speed of sound to turn delay into distance.
reading: Shout across a canyon and a moment later the canyon shouts back. The delay is the round trip of your sound to the far wall and back. If you know the speed of sound, you can measure the distance without a tape: distance equals speed times time, divided by two because the sound went there and back. A 2-second echo in air means the wall is about 343 meters away.

*Sonar* does this on purpose, under water. A ship sends a sharp click downward and listens. In seawater, sound travels about 1,500 meters per second, so an echo that returns after 4 seconds came from a bottom about 3,000 meters down. Sweeping the click across the seafloor maps mountains and trenches that no one can see. Sonar was developed after the sinking of the Titanic in 1912 and during the First World War to find icebergs and submarines, and it still does both.

Bats invented the method millions of years earlier. A hunting bat squeaks at frequencies up to about 100,000 hertz, far above human hearing, and listens for the echo from a moth. Its calls are high-pitched because short wavelengths bounce off small objects that long waves would pass around. Dolphins do the same with clicks under water. The site's drum bench lets you try a slow version: tap once and listen for the return from the far wall of the room.

*Ultrasound* in a doctor's office is sonar at very small scale. A probe sends pulses into the body and times the echoes from organs and from a baby's heartbeat, building a picture out of nothing but delay. Sound is a safer choice than X-rays for this job because it carries far less energy per wave.

words.d: finding objects under water by sending sound and timing the echo
the way bats and dolphins find things by listening to echoes of their own calls
sound too high for humans to hear, used to make images inside the body

look.title: Sonar Echo Time and Depth
look.cite: calculated from about 1,500 m/s in seawater, rounded
look.prompt: Why is the depth for each row half of the speed times the time? What would go wrong if the water were much warmer than expected?

check.q: A ship's sonar ping returns after 2 seconds. With sound at about 1,500 m/s in seawater, how deep is the bottom?
choices: 3,000 meters
750 meters
6,000 meters
1,500 meters
check.why: The sound went down and back, so divide the round trip by two: 1,500 times 2 seconds is 3,000 meters there and back, or 1,500 meters deep.

check.q: Why do bats use very high-frequency calls for echolocation?
choices: Short wavelengths bounce off small prey like moths
High sounds travel faster
High sounds travel farther
Moths cannot hear any sound
check.why: A wave tends to pass around objects smaller than its wavelength. Short, high-frequency waves reflect from small insects.

check.q: Why is ultrasound rather than X-rays used to look at a baby before birth?
choices: Ultrasound is faster
Sound waves carry far less energy per wave than X-rays and do not damage cells
X-rays cannot pass through skin
Ultrasound is in color
check.why: X-rays are high-energy and can harm cells. Ultrasound builds a picture from gentle echoes.

lessons.title: Radar and the Weather Map
lessons.mainIdea: Radar sends radio waves and times the echo, and the tiny frequency shift of a moving target reveals its speed, which is how weather radar tracks storms.
reading: *Radar* is sonar with radio waves. A dish sends a pulse of microwaves and listens for the reflection. Because the waves travel at the speed of light, the timing is fierce: an echo from an airplane 15 kilometers away returns in one ten-thousandth of a second. Electronics measure that easily, and a rotating dish turns the delays into dots on a screen. Radar was developed in Britain and the United States during the 1930s, and by 1940 it was warning of approaching aircraft.

Raindrops reflect microwaves too. Weather radar sends pulses into the sky and paints a map of where rain and hail are, colored by how strong the echo is. Watch a Chicago forecast and the green, yellow and red blotches sliding across Illinois are radar echoes, updated every few minutes.

Modern weather radar does something more. When a wave reflects from an object moving toward the dish, the returning wave is squeezed to a slightly higher frequency. From an object moving away, it is stretched lower. This is the *Doppler effect*, the same reason a passing siren drops in pitch. By measuring the shift, Doppler radar sees which way the rain is moving inside a storm. A patch of echoes rushing toward the dish right beside a patch rushing away means a rotating column. That is a possible tornado, and the warning goes out before the funnel touches down.

Every technology in this unit is the same idea wearing different clothes. Send a wave, or catch one that is already there. Measure its amplitude, its timing, its frequency. Turn the measurements into information. The turntable does it with a groove, the eye with a lens, the bat with a squeak and the weather service with a spinning dish.

words.d: finding objects by sending radio waves and timing the echo
the change in frequency of a wave when its source or reflector is moving toward or away from you

look.title: The Siren on Lake Shore Drive
look.text: An ambulance races past a student waiting at a crosswalk. As it approaches, the siren sounds high and urgent. The instant it passes, the pitch drops, though the driver never touched the siren. A weather radar in the suburbs uses the very same effect to see wind inside a thunderstorm.
look.prompt: Explain what happens to the sound waves reaching the student as the ambulance approaches and then moves away. How does radar use this to spot a rotating storm?

check.q: What does weather radar actually detect when it shows rain on a map?
choices: Sounds of thunder
Light from lightning
Microwave echoes reflected from raindrops and hail
Heat from the storm
check.why: The radar sends microwave pulses and records where they bounce back. Raindrops reflect them, and stronger echoes mean heavier rain.

check.q: A reflected wave returns at a higher frequency than it was sent. What does that tell the radar?
choices: The object is very large
The object is very far away
The object is made of metal
The object is moving toward the radar
check.why: Motion toward the dish squeezes the returning waves to a higher frequency. That is the Doppler effect.

check.q: Why can radar measure distances to aircraft while sonar is used for the sea floor?
choices: Radio waves travel through air but sound works better in water, and each is matched to its medium
Radar is louder
Sound cannot travel through air
Radio waves cannot travel through air
check.why: Radio waves are strongly absorbed by seawater but travel freely through air. Sound travels well through water. Each tool uses the wave that survives the trip.

review.q: In a compound microscope, what is the job of the objective lens?
choices: To light the specimen
To hold the slide flat
To reflect light to the eyepiece
To form the first magnified image of the specimen
review.why: The objective, nearest the specimen, makes a magnified image inside the tube. The eyepiece then magnifies that image again.

review.q: Why are the largest telescopes reflectors rather than refractors?
choices: A mirror can be supported from behind and made very large without sagging
Mirrors are more transparent than lenses
Lenses cannot be curved
Reflectors do not need to be pointed
review.why: A lens can only be held at its edge and bends under its own weight past about a meter. A mirror can be huge.

review.q: Which lists the electromagnetic spectrum from longest wavelength to shortest?
choices: X-rays, visible, infrared, radio
Radio, infrared, visible, X-rays
Visible, radio, X-rays, infrared
Infrared, radio, visible, X-rays
review.why: Radio waves are the longest, then infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and finally gamma rays.

review.q: The Webb telescope observes in infrared partly because:
choices: Infrared is the brightest kind of light
Its mirror cannot reflect visible light
Light from the most distant galaxies has been stretched into the infrared
Infrared travels faster than visible light
review.why: The expansion of the universe stretches the light of early galaxies to longer wavelengths, into the infrared.

review.q: A digital signal resists noise better than an analog one because:
choices: Digital signals cannot be scratched
Digital signals are always stronger
Digital signals use no electricity
The receiver only needs to tell high from low, so small noise is ignored
review.why: Bits are ones and zeros. Noise that does not flip a bit is simply discarded, and check bits catch flips that do happen.

review.q: Which happens first when a phone sends a photo?
choices: The camera measures red, green and blue light at each pixel and stores numbers
The picture is sent as light through a fiber
The friend's screen lights up its pixels
The cell tower forwards the packets
review.why: The image must be turned into numbers before it can be compressed, packaged and transmitted.

review.q: What keeps a light pulse inside an optical fiber over many kilometers?
choices: A vacuum inside the glass
Total internal reflection at the boundary of the core
The pulse is too weak to leave
Copper wrapped around the glass
review.why: Light in the glass core strikes the boundary at a shallow angle and reflects completely back in, again and again.

review.q: A sonar echo returns after 6 seconds in seawater at about 1,500 m/s. How deep is the bottom?
choices: 9,000 meters
1,500 meters
4,500 meters
250 meters
review.why: The round trip is 1,500 times 6, or 9,000 meters. The sound went down and back, so the depth is half: 4,500 meters.
